story.title: Execution by Firing Squad Approved for Fort Hood Shooter Nidal Hasan
story.summary: Nidal Malik Hasan, the former Army psychiatrist responsible for the 2009 Fort Hood shooting that killed 13 people, is set to be executed by firing squad. This decision marks the first military execution by firing squad in the United States since World War II. The execution plan has been approved by the Trump administration and confirmed by the Pentagon.

explore_lenses.label: How did Hasan’s case reach this point?
explore_lenses.title: A 13-year military trial and appeals process
explore_lenses.summary: Hasan’s death sentence followed a 2013 court-martial and the mandatory military appellate process for capital cases. His last direct Supreme Court appeal ended in March 2025.

claims.text: A military panel convicted Hasan of 13 premeditated murders and 32 attempted premeditated murders, then sentenced him to death, dismissal, and forfeiture of pay and allowances in 2013.
The Court of Appeals for the Armed Forces affirmed the conviction and sentence on March 4, 2024; the Supreme Court denied Hasan’s certiorari petition on March 31, 2025.

Hasan’s lawyers argued that closing part of a trial proceeding to the public violated his Sixth Amendment public-trial right and required a remedy; the military appeals court ultimately affirmed the case rather than grant relief.

explore_lenses.label: Why is a firing-squad order significant?
explore_lenses.title: A break with decades of military practice
explore_lenses.summary: If carried out, the execution would end a military-execution hiatus dating to 1961 and use a method the military has not used since World War II.

claims.text: The Army’s legal publication says the military has not carried out a death sentence since Army Pvt. John Bennett was hanged in 1961.
News reporting identifies the last known U.S. military execution by firing squad, described as execution by musketry, as occurring in November 1945.
The Army’s 2026 legal review said four prisoners were then on military death row, underscoring that a presidentially approved execution would be unusual even within the military justice system.

explore_lenses.label: What must happen before an execution?
explore_lenses.title: The Army secretary must set the logistics
explore_lenses.summary: The president’s approval is legally necessary for a court-martial death sentence, but the Pentagon says the Army secretary still must set the execution’s time and place.

claims.text: Federal military law provides that a court-martial death sentence cannot be executed until the president approves it; it also provides that execution follows completion of appellate review under service regulations.

Pentagon spokesman Sean Parnell said Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth recommended execution by an Army firing squad, President Trump approved the recommendation, and the secretary of the Army will set the time and place.
No execution date or location had been announced in the reporting available as of October 6, 2026.

story_report.summary: President Trump has approved the execution of Nidal Malik Hasan by an Army firing squad after Hasan was convicted in the 2009 Fort Hood shooting, in which 13 people were killed and 32 injured. Pentagon spokesman Sean Parnell said Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth recommended the method and Trump approved it. The decision clears the way for the secretary of the Army to set the execution’s time and place, following the completion of appellate review required under military law.

sections.heading: Hasan Conviction and Appeals
sections.body: A military panel in 2013 convicted Hasan of 13 counts of premeditated murder and 32 counts of attempted premeditated murder. It sentenced him to death, dismissal from service, and forfeiture of pay and allowances. The Court of Appeals for the Armed Forces affirmed the conviction and sentence on March 4, 2024, and the Supreme Court denied Hasan’s petition for review on March 31, 2025. Hasan’s lawyers had argued that closure of part of the trial violated his Sixth Amendment right to a public trial, but the military appeals court affirmed the case.

sections.heading: Military Execution History
sections.body: The planned firing-squad execution would be the U.S. military’s first such execution since World War II; news reporting identifies the last known execution by musketry as occurring in November 1945. More broadly, the Army has not carried out any death sentence since Pvt. John Bennett was hanged in 1961, according to an Army legal publication. That publication said four prisoners were on military death row in 2026, making a presidentially approved execution rare within the military justice system.

unresolved.text: No execution date or location had been announced in reporting available as of October 6, 2026. The public materials also did not specify the firing-squad protocol or explain why that method was selected.
The supplied reporting does not establish whether Hasan will pursue further collateral litigation after the execution order.

related_stories.title: Nationwide Protests Erupt in France Over Education Funding
related_stories.summary: Protests across France have intensified as students demand increased funding for education, leading to significant unrest. Demonstrators have blockaded schools and clashed with police, resulting in the heaviest toll from student protests in decades. The movement, which began in low-income suburbs, has drawn tens of thousands of participants, including teachers and trade unions, aiming to transform the protests into a major social movement against the government of outgoing President Emmanuel Macron.

related_stories.title: Russia Addresses Death of Anti-Plague Institute Worker Amid Calls for Transparency
related_stories.summary: Russian authorities are investigating the death of a worker at an anti-plague institute in Irkutsk, which has been attributed to pneumonia. Regional Governor Igor Kobzev stated that an inspection by the health watchdog confirmed the cause of death. Meanwhile, US Secretary of State Marco Rubio has urged Russia to be transparent about the findings related to this incident.

related_stories.title: British National Arrested in Connection with RAF Fairford Incident
related_stories.summary: A 22-year-old British national was arrested in London on suspicion of preparing terrorist acts related to an incident at RAF Fairford airbase. This marks the seventh arrest in connection with the ongoing investigation, following the release of other suspects on bail.
